chapter_title: Implementing an ERC-20 Token in Solidity

screens.title: Implementing an ERC-20 Token in Solidity
screens.subtitle: From local setup to deployed token — build, secure, and ship a fungible token using OpenZeppelin and Hardhat

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn to build a production-minded ERC-20 token using OpenZeppelin and Hardhat. We'll start by creating a local Hardhat project and installing the OpenZeppelin Contracts library, then write a Solidity contract that inherits ERC20 and Ownable, mint an initial supply properly converted to base units, and add optional mint and burn functions. Next you'll author a deployment script, configure networks and environment variables, and deploy locally before moving to a public testnet such as Sepolia. Along the way we'll highlight two common pitfalls: forgetting to multiply by ten to the power of decimals, and exposing mint functionality without access control. By the end you'll be ready to deploy a test token and interact with it using ethers. js or Etherscan. For a concrete example you'll create a MyToken contract that mints one million tokens to the deployer, then deploy it to a local Hardhat node and later to Sepolia with environment-based credentials. Keep an eye on supply mechanics and access control — they determine whether your token behaves as intended or becomes vulnerable to inflation.

keyIdea.title: Build securely with libraries and tooling
keyIdea.text: Use Hardhat for development and OpenZeppelin Contracts for audited ERC-20 logic. Focus on correct numeric conversions and access control when minting or burning tokens.

screens.title: Initialize a Hardhat Project
screens.subtitle: Create a reproducible dev environment for building and testing your token

narration.text: A stable local environment is the foundation of safe token development. Start by making a project folder, initializing npm, installing Hardhat as a dev dependency, and running npx hardhat to scaffold a project. Choosing JavaScript or TypeScript will guide the sample files you receive. Hardhat gives you a local node for quick tests and a consistent compilation pipeline so your Solidity code compiles the same way every time. For example, run mkdir my-erc20-token, npm init -y, npm install --save-dev hardhat, and then npx hardhat to create the project. This setup matters because it allows you to iterate quickly: deploy contracts to a local node, run scripts, and write unit tests that exercise mint and burn behavior without spending real funds. A common misconception is that local nodes are optional; they are essential to validate numeric conversions, event emission, and access control before pushing to a public network. As a quick check, after scaffolding run npx hardhat node and then run a deploy script against localhost to ensure your scripts connect and print addresses. What will you verify first when your local deployment completes?

keyIdea.title: Reproducible local development
keyIdea.text: Hardhat creates a consistent workbench: compile, test, and run scripts locally before public deployment.

screens.title: Install OpenZeppelin Contracts
screens.subtitle: Use audited building blocks for ERC-20 and access control

narration.text: OpenZeppelin Contracts provide audited implementations of common patterns, including ERC-20 and Ownable. Installing @openzeppelin/contracts is a small step that greatly reduces security risk because these contracts implement standard behavior and have been reviewed by many developers. Install the package using npm install @openzeppelin/contracts. Once installed, you will import the ERC20 and Ownable contracts into your Solidity file and inherit from them. For example, importing ERC20 gives you standard functions like transfer, approve, and balanceOf without re-implementing them. Ownable provides a simple owner pattern and the onlyOwner modifier to protect privileged functions. A concrete example is adding Ownable to enable an owner-only mint function: the owner can mint new tokens, while other addresses cannot. A common misconception is that using a library absolves you from understanding internal behavior — you must still know how _mint and _burn affect total supply and balances, and how decimals interact with human-readable amounts. In short, add OpenZeppelin to save time and improve safety, but audit your own custom additions. Install OpenZeppelin Contracts means openzeppelin reduces implementation risk; always inspect any custom code that wraps or extends library functions.. In practical terms, use audited building blocks for erc-20 and access control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: MyToken.sol — Contract Structure
screens.subtitle: Understand inheritance, constructor, and the initial mint pattern

narration.text: Let's examine the provided MyToken contract to see how it uses inheritance and the constructor to establish name, symbol, owner, and initial supply. The contract inherits ERC20 and Ownable so it gets standard token behavior and a simple owner-based access control mechanism. In the constructor the ERC20 parent receives the name and symbol. The constructor then mints the initialSupply converted to base units by multiplying by ten to the power of decimals. This conversion is critical: Solidity stores token amounts as integers representing the smallest unit. The example mints the supply to msg. sender, which keeps the deployer as the initial holder. One misconception is assuming initialSupply passed to the constructor is already in base units; the provided pattern expects a human-readable initialSupply and converts it. A practical check is to deploy locally with an initialSupply of 1000000 and then query balanceOf(deployer) in the local console—if you see 1000000 times 10 to the decimals, the conversion is correct. Reviewing the inheritance and constructor initialization clarifies where state is set and who controls future minting or burning. MyToken.sol — Contract Structure means initialize erc20 with name/symbol, set owner, and mint initial supply after converting to base units using decimals().. In practical terms, understand inheritance, constructor, and the initial mint pattern. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Constructor sets state and converts units

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › MyToken.sol — Contract Structure
MyToken.sol — Contract Structure
Inheritance, constructor, and initial mint explained.
Core contract (excerpt)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

import "@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/ERC20.sol";
import "@openzeppelin/contracts/access/Ownable.sol"; // For basic access control

contract MyToken is ERC20, Ownable {
    constructor(string memory name_, string memory symbol_, uint256 initialSupply_)
        ERC20(name_, symbol_)
        Ownable(msg.sender) // The deployer is the owner
    {
        // Mint the initial supply to the contract deployer
        // initialSupply_ is in human-readable units, convert to base units
        _mint(msg.sender, initialSupply_ * (10 ** decimals()));
    }
}
Annotations
  • ERC20(name, symbol): initializes token metadata and decimals behavior.
  • Ownable(msg.sender): sets the deployer as owner for owner-only functions.
  • _mint(...): creates tokens in the smallest unit; use decimals() to convert human amounts.
Misconception
Passing initialSupply already multiplied by decimals will double-scale amounts if you also multiply in the constructor. Decide one convention and be consistent.
Example
If decimals() returns 18, _mint(msg.sender, 1000 * (10 ** 18)) mints one thousand tokens in base units.
Check
After deploying locally, query balanceOf(deployer) to confirm the expected base-unit balance.
Takeaway
Constructor responsibilities: initialize parents, set owner, and mint correctly converted initial supply.

screens.title: Mint and Burn — Function Behavior & Access Control
screens.subtitle: Allowing supply changes safely with owner-only minting and public burning

narration.text: Mint and burn functions change the token supply and therefore must be designed carefully. In the MyToken example a public mint function exists but is guarded with onlyOwner, which means only the deployer — the owner — can mint more tokens. This prevents uncontrolled inflation that would devalue existing tokens. The burn function allows any token holder to destroy their own tokens, reducing supply. A clear claim: mint must be restricted and burn can be public or permissioned depending on your token economics. A concrete example: if the owner calls mint(to, amount) with 100 * (10 ** decimals()), supply increases by that base-unit amount and the recipient's balance grows. A common mistake is making mint callable by anyone; that opens an uncontrolled supply vulnerability and immediate hyperinflation. Another misconception is thinking burn requires special ownership — burning from the caller's balance is typically allowed. Closing question: when would you choose to make burn restricted to a governance process versus allowing any holder to burn their tokens? Mint and Burn — Function Behavior & Access Control means protect mint with onlyowner or similar access control. design burn rules according to token economics and governance.. In practical terms, allowing supply changes safely with owner-only minting and public burning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Control supply with permissions
keyIdea.text: Protect mint with onlyOwner or similar access control. Design burn rules according to token economics and governance.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Mint and Burn — Function Behavior & Access Control
Mint and Burn — Function Behavior & Access Control
Who can change supply and why that matters.
Functions in MyToken
// Optional: Add a function to allow the owner to mint more tokens
function mint(address to, uint256 amount) public onlyOwner {
    _mint(to, amount);
}

// Optional: Add a function to allow burning tokens
function burn(uint256 amount) public {
    _burn(msg.sender, amount);
}
Practical notes
  • Mint onlyOwner: prevents anyone from increasing supply arbitrarily.
  • Burn from caller: lets holders reduce their balance and total supply.
  • Accounting: _mint and _burn update balances and totalSupply atomically.
Warning
If mint lacks onlyOwner, anyone can create supply and destroy the token's economic value.
Example
Owner calls mint(alice, 50 * 10**decimals()) to top up Alice's balance in base units.
Misconception
Thinking public mint is safe if limits exist in UI — limits must be enforced in contract code.
Takeaway
Protect supply-changing functions with on-chain access control; design burns according to token policy.

screens.title: Deployment Script — deploy.js Explained
screens.subtitle: Use ethers and Hardhat to publish the contract and inspect balances

narration.text: A deployment script ties your compiled contract to a concrete network and prints useful state so you can verify success. The example deploy. js uses ethers from Hardhat to get signers, compile the factory, deploy MyToken with a name, symbol, and initialSupply, then wait for deployment and log addresses and balances. It also shows how to format balances for human-readability using formatUnits and formatEther. Running this script against a local node prints the deployer account and token balances so you can confirm the mint occurred. When moving to a public testnet the same script runs, but you must configure hardhat. config. js and use environment variables for RPC URLs and private keys. A common mistake is forgetting to call waitForDeployment or an equivalent, which can cause scripts to query state before the transaction is mined. As a practical check, run the script locally, then call balanceOf on the deployed contract and compare the result to your expected initial supply multiplied by decimals. This confirms both deployment and scaling are correct. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Deployment Script — deploy.js Explained
deploy.js — Key steps
Deploy the contract and confirm balances via ethers utilities.
Deploy script (excerpt)
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const [deployer] = await ethers.getSigners();

  console.log("Deploying contracts with the account:", deployer.address);

  const initialSupply = 1000000; // 1 million tokens
  const MyToken = await ethers.getContractFactory("MyToken");
  const myToken = await MyToken.deploy("Cohortia Token", "CHT", initialSupply);

  await myToken.waitForDeployment();

  console.log("MyToken deployed to:", myToken.target);
  console.log("Deployer balance:", ethers.formatEther(await deployer.getBalance()));
  console.log("Token deployer balance:", ethers.formatUnits(await myToken.balanceOf(deployer.address), await myToken.decimals()));
}
Notes
  • getSigners: provides accounts from the network for deploying transactions.
  • formatUnits: converts token base units back to human-readable amounts using decimals.
  • waitForDeployment: ensures the deployment completes before querying state.
Pro tip
Log both native balance and token balance to confirm gas and token state after deployment.
Example
Running the script locally prints deployer address and the expected token balance equal to initialSupply.
Common mistake
Querying token decimals incorrectly leads to wrong human-readable formatting—use myToken.decimals() when calling formatUnits.
Takeaway
A deployment script is your single source of truth for reproducible publishes and initial state verification.

screens.title: Configure Networks and Environment Variables
screens.subtitle: Set RPC URLs and private keys securely before deploying to Sepolia

narration.text: When deploying to a public testnet you must configure network entries in hardhat. config. js and supply credentials via environment variables. The sample hardhat. config. js declares a sepolia network using process. env. SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and process. env. PRIVATE_KEY. Create a. env file and load it with dotenv so your deployment scripts can access the variables without embedding secrets in source control. For example, set SEPOLIA_RPC_URL to your provider endpoint and PRIVATE_KEY to the deployer's private key locally; then add. env to. gitignore. This pattern matters because exposing private keys in code is a critical security risk. A common incorrect practice is pasting the private key directly into hardhat. config. js. Instead, use process. env and environment management. Also include etherscan A P I keys for verification when needed. As a practical verification, attempt a dry run to Sepolia with a deploy script and confirm the transaction is sent, then later verify the code on the explorer using your configured A P I key. Configure Networks and Environment Variables means use dotenv and environment variables for rpc endpoints and private keys; never commit private keys to version control.. In practical terms, set rpc urls and private keys securely before deploying to sepolia. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Keep secrets out of source

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Configure Networks and Environment Variables
Configure Networks & Env
Use env variables for RPC and private keys before public deployments.
hardhat.config.js (excerpt)
require("@nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox");
require("dotenv").config();

const SEPOLIA_RPC_URL = process.env.SEPOLIA_RPC_URL;
const PRIVATE_KEY = process.env.PRIVATE_KEY;

module.exports = {
  solidity: "0.8.20",
  networks: {
    sepolia: {
      url: SEPOLIA_RPC_URL || "",
      accounts: PRIVATE_KEY !== undefined ? [PRIVATE_KEY] : [],
      chainId: 11155111,
    },
    localhost: {
      url: "http://127.0.0.1:8545/",
      chainId: 31337,
    }
  },
};
.env example
SEPOLIA_RPC_URL="YOUR_INFURA_OR_ALCHEMY_URL"
PRIVATE_KEY="YOUR_METAMASK_PRIVATE_KEY"
ETHERSCAN_API_KEY="YOUR_ETHERSCAN_API_KEY"
Ensure .env is in .gitignore and never commit your PRIVATE_KEY to source control.
Example
Deploy to sepolia after configuring SEPOLIA_RPC_URL and PRIVATE_KEY in .env, then run the deploy script with --network sepolia.
Common error
Missing or malformed RPC URL will prevent your script from connecting. Confirm URL and key syntax.
Takeaway
Separate configuration from code and use environment variables for secrets and endpoints.

screens.title: Deploy Locally, Then to Sepolia
screens.subtitle: Test on a local node first, then run the same scripts against a testnet

narration.text: A best practice is to deploy first to your local Hardhat node and confirm contract behavior, then deploy to a public testnet like Sepolia once tests pass. Locally, start npx hardhat node, then run npx hardhat run scripts/deploy. js --network localhost to execute your deploy script against the local node. Inspect logs for deployer address, native balance, and token balance. Once local verification is successful, update hardhat. config. js with your Sepolia RPC and private key and run npx hardhat run scripts/deploy. js --network sepolia. Use the printed contract address to inspect the deployment on the testnet explorer. One misconception is thinking that passing the same private key to multiple networks is risky; it's acceptable for test keys but never reuse production keys. Also remember to verify contract source on the explorer with your A P I key so the contract is recognized as an ERC-20. After deployment, test read functions like decimals and balanceOf and, if you implemented mint, call mint from the owner's address to verify access control. Deploy Locally, Then to Sepolia means deploy locally first to validate behavior, then run the same steps on a testnet to confirm cross-network compatibility.. In practical terms, test on a local node first, then run the same scripts against a testnet. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Interact with Your Token: ethers.js and Etherscan
screens.subtitle: Read state and execute transactions after deployment

narration.text: After deployment you will interact with your token either programmatically using ethers. js or via the explorer's read and write tabs. With ethers. js, get a contract factory or attach to an existing address, then call decimals(), balanceOf(address), transfer and other standard functions. The deployed contract in the example exposes decimals and balanceOf; formatUnits converts base units to human amounts for logging. On Etherscan you can use the Read Contract tab to query decimals and balances and, with a connected wallet, use Write Contract to call owner-limited functions like mint. A common pitfall is attempting to call an owner-only function from a non-owner account; this will revert. Programmatically, ensure your signer is the owner when calling mint. Practically, after deploying to Sepolia, try calling balanceOf for the deployer and then, if you implemented mint, call mint from the owner to another address and verify the balance increase. This demonstrates that on-chain access control and unit conversions are functioning as intended. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Security Pitfalls
screens.subtitle: Decimals, access control, and deployment configuration errors to avoid

narration.text: There are three recurring mistakes when implementing ERC-20 tokens: incorrect unit conversion, insufficient access control, and exposing secrets in configuration. First, failing to multiply by ten to the power of decimals results in balances that are off by a large factor; always convert human-readable amounts to base units when calling _mint. Second, leaving mint public or otherwise unprotected allows arbitrary creation of tokens, destroying the token's economic value; protect supply-changing functions with onlyOwner or a governance check. Third, embedding private keys or RPC URLs in code can leak credentials when pushing to version control; use environment variables and. gitignore. A helpful way to compare is to run three checks before deployment: 1) deploy locally and confirm balanceOf matches expected base-unit amount; 2) attempt to call mint from a non-owner account to ensure it reverts; 3) confirm your. env is not committed. A misconception is assuming wallets will protect you from code-level mistakes—wallets protect keys, but contract code must be correct. Ending question: which of these checks will you add to your CI pipeline to stop regressions? Common Mistakes and Security Pitfalls means verify unit conversion, enforce access control, and secure credentials before deploying to a public network.. In practical terms, decimals, access control, and deployment configuration errors to avoid. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Common Mistakes and Security Pitfalls
Common Mistakes & Security Pitfalls
Three areas to double-check before any deploy.
Decimals conversion
Always multiply human amounts by 10**decimals() when calling _mint. Forgetting this produces values off by large orders of magnitude.
Access control
Restrict mint to owner or governance. Public mint functions enable uncontrolled inflation and immediate devaluation.
Configuration secrets
Never commit PRIVATE_KEY or RPC URLs. Use dotenv and ignore .env in version control to avoid leaking credentials.
Quick tests
Local deploy → confirm balance; non-owner mint call → expect revert; verify .env not committed.
Misconception
Relying on UI controls alone to restrict actions is insufficient—contracts enforce rules on-chain.
Takeaway
Add unit, access, and configuration checks to your deployment checklist to prevent costly mistakes.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Hands-on Activity: Deploy Your Custom ERC-20
Hands-on Activity
Checklist to build, test, and deploy MyToken.
Quick checklist
  1. Initialize project and install dependencies (Hardhat, @openzeppelin/contracts, dotenv).
  2. Create contracts/MyToken.sol using ERC20 and Ownable and add mint/burn.
  3. Create scripts/deploy.js that deploys and prints balances in human units.
  4. Configure hardhat.config.js and .env for Sepolia; never commit private keys.
  5. Deploy locally, verify, then deploy to Sepolia and verify on the explorer.
Extension challenge
Add OpenZeppelin's Pausable contract to MyToken and provide an owner-only pause/unpause API. Test that transfers revert while paused and succeed when unpaused.
Why it matters
A pause mechanism gives an emergency tool to halt activity during incidents, but it must be constrained to trusted governance to avoid centralization risks.
Verification step
After Sepolia deploy, verify contract on the explorer and confirm it's recognized as ERC-20.
Hands-on check
Call balanceOf and decimals via ethers.js and compare formatted results to expected values.
Takeaway
Completing this flow gives you a deployable ERC-20 with verifiable behavior and a clear extension for emergency control.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders from this chapter

narration.text: Keep three core concepts in mind as you build an ERC-20 token. First, use OpenZeppelin Contracts to rely on audited, standard implementations for ERC-20 and access control. This reduces the chance of reintroducing common errors. Second, always multiply human-readable token amounts by ten to the power of decimals to convert to base units before calling _mint; failing to do so will produce incorrect balances. Third, secure any supply-changing functions with robust access control such as onlyOwner; leaving mint public creates an uncontrolled supply vulnerability. Together these practices help you produce a token that behaves correctly, maintains economic integrity, and can be safely deployed and verified on testnets and explorers. Which of these will you prioritize in your next token project? screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three practical checks before publishing a token

narration.text: Before you publish a token, run these three practical checks: verify unit conversion for all minting paths, confirm access control prevents unauthorized minting, and ensure your deployment configuration keeps private keys out of source control. These checks prevent common failures where tokens either have incorrect balances due to unit mistakes, suffer hyperinflation due to open minting, or expose credentials that enable theft. After confirming these items locally and on a testnet, you will be ready to verify the contract on a block explorer and interact with it using ethers. js or the explorer's write interface. Carry these checks into your future token work to maintain safety and trust for users of your token. What to Remember
A short pre-deploy checklist for token safety.
Unit conversion
Confirm initialSupply uses decimals correctly.
Access control
Ensure mint is restricted to trusted accounts.
Secrets management
Use .env and ignore files; never commit private keys.
Final takeaway

Run a local deployment, test access control and unit conversion, and only then deploy to a public testnet. These steps preserve correctness and trust in your token.
